title: Information Security: Attacks and Safe Banking
summary: Building on cyber security basics: the malware families and attack types exams name, how to spot a phishing message, the scams that specifically target bank customers and what a bank will never ask, and a practical defence checklist.
learningObjectives: Classify the common malware families by how each spreads and what it does.
Name the main attack types, including social-engineering variants, MITM and DoS.
Work through the signs that a message is phishing.
State what a bank will never ask a customer for, and list the everyday defences.

blocks.title: Where this fits
blocks.markdown:
This topic assumes the cyber-security-basics ground — the CIA triad, authentication vs authorisation, MFA, and encryption vs hashing. Here the focus is narrower and more practical: **naming the attacks** exams list, **spotting a phishing message**, and the **frauds aimed at bank customers**.

One recurring exam idea: most successful attacks on individuals are **social engineering** — tricking a person — not code that breaks a technical control. The defence is largely habit.

blocks.title: Malware families
blocks.markdown:
**Malware** is any software written to harm or misuse a system.

| Type | How it spreads / what it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Virus** | attaches to a host file; spreads when that file is run and shared |
| **Worm** | self-replicates across a network on its own, no host file, no user action |
| **Trojan** | disguised as something useful; runs when the user opens it; does not self-replicate |
| **Ransomware** | encrypts the victim's files and demands payment for the key |
| **Spyware** | secretly records activity and sends it to the attacker |
| **Keylogger** | a form of spyware that captures keystrokes, including passwords and OTPs |
| **Adware** | forces unwanted adverts; often bundled with free software |
| **Rootkit** | hides deep in the system to conceal other malware and resist removal |
| **Botnet** | a network of compromised machines controlled remotely for spam or DDoS |

The dividing line examiners test: **a worm self-replicates and needs no host or user action; a virus needs a host file and user action; a Trojan does not self-replicate at all.**

blocks.title: Attack types
blocks.markdown:
- **Phishing:** a fraudulent message impersonating a trusted body to steal credentials or plant malware. **Spear phishing** targets one named person; **vishing** is by phone call, **smishing** by SMS.
- **Social engineering (general):** pretexting (inventing a scenario), baiting (leaving infected media), tailgating (following someone through a secure door).
- **Brute force:** trying every possible password. **Dictionary attack:** trying a list of likely passwords. **Credential stuffing:** reusing username/password pairs leaked from another site.
- **Man-in-the-middle (MITM):** an attacker secretly relays and can alter traffic between two parties — a risk on open Wi-Fi; HTTPS defeats the common form.
- **Denial of Service (DoS)** and **Distributed DoS (DDoS):** flooding a service with traffic so real users cannot reach it; DDoS uses many machines (often a botnet).
- **SQL injection:** feeding crafted input into a web form so it is treated as database commands — a server-side flaw, not a user mistake.
- **Shoulder surfing:** simply watching someone type a PIN or password.

blocks.title: Worked example: is this email phishing?
blocks.markdown:
> **From:** "Bank Security" <alerts@secure-bank-verify.com>
> **Subject:** URGENT: your account will be blocked in 24 hours
>
> Dear Customer, we detected an unusual login. To avoid suspension, verify your details now: **[Verify Account]** (link points to `http://secure-bank-verify.com/login`). Enter your card number, PIN and the OTP sent to your phone. — Bank Security Team

Work through the signs:

1. **Sender domain.** `secure-bank-verify.com` is not the bank's real domain. A display name of "Bank Security" proves nothing.
2. **Urgency and threat.** "blocked in 24 hours" pressures you to act before thinking — a standard tactic.
3. **Generic greeting.** "Dear Customer", not your name.
4. **Link mismatch.** Hover: the visible text says "Verify Account" but the URL is an unrelated `http://` (not even HTTPS) address.
5. **Asks for secrets.** Card number, PIN and OTP together — no legitimate bank page asks for all three.

**Verdict: phishing.** Do not click. Reach the bank through its official app or a number printed on your card.

blocks.title: Scams aimed at bank customers
blocks.markdown:
**What a bank will never ask you for:** your full card number by email or call, your **PIN**, **CVV**, **online-banking password**, or an **OTP**. Anyone asking for these is an attacker, even if they know your name and last transaction.

Common frauds:

- **OTP / "verification code" call:** a caller claiming to be from the bank asks you to read out the code you just received. That code authorises *their* transaction.
- **Fake KYC-update link:** an SMS or email says your account will be frozen unless you "complete KYC" through a link. The link leads to a credential-harvesting page.
- **Remote-access app:** you are told to install a screen-sharing app "so support can help", which lets the fraudster see your screen and control the device.
- **UPI collect-request trick:** you are sent a *request-money* notification dressed up as "receive your refund — enter your PIN to accept". Approving it pays them. **You never enter a PIN to receive money.**
- **QR code to receive money:** scanning a QR and entering a PIN sends money out, it does not bring money in.

blocks.title: Everyday defences
blocks.markdown:
- **Multi-factor authentication** on every account that offers it — a stolen password alone then is not enough.
- **Unique, long passwords** kept in a **password manager**; never reuse the banking password anywhere else.
- **Patch promptly** — operating system, browser and apps; many attacks use flaws already fixed.
- **Antivirus** for known malware and a **firewall** at the boundary; neither replaces the other.
- **Backups** on the 3-2-1 pattern (3 copies, 2 media, 1 off-site/offline) — the real defence against ransomware.
- **Check before you trust:** the sender's real address, the padlock and exact domain in the address bar, and reach the bank only through its official app or a printed number.
- **Avoid banking on open public Wi-Fi;** if unavoidable, use a **VPN**.
- **Lock devices** with a PIN/biometric and enable remote wipe.

blocks.title: Common confusions
blocks.markdown:
- **A worm spreads by itself; a virus needs a host file and a user action; a Trojan never self-replicates.**
- **Phishing is the message; vishing is by call, smishing by SMS; spear phishing is targeted.**
- **A DoS floods one service from one source; a DDoS floods it from many** (usually a botnet).
- **SQL injection is a server-side coding flaw**, not something a careful user can prevent by being cautious.
- **A firewall filters traffic at a boundary; antivirus removes malware on the machine.** Different jobs.
- **HTTPS stops the common man-in-the-middle**, but it does not vouch that the site owner is honest.
- **You never enter a UPI PIN to *receive* money** — a PIN only authorises money going out.

blocks.title: Quick revision
blocks.markdown:
- Malware: virus (host + action), worm (self-spreads on a network), Trojan (disguised, no self-replication), ransomware (encrypts for payment), spyware/keylogger, adware, rootkit (hides), botnet (remote army).
- Attacks: phishing/spear/vishing/smishing, pretexting/baiting/tailgating, brute force vs dictionary vs credential stuffing, MITM, DoS/DDoS, SQL injection (server-side), shoulder surfing.
- Phishing signs: wrong sender domain, urgency/threat, generic greeting, link text vs real URL mismatch, asks for PIN/CVV/OTP.
- A bank never asks for card number, PIN, CVV, password or OTP. You never enter a PIN to receive money.
- Defences: MFA, unique passwords + manager, prompt patching, antivirus + firewall, 3-2-1 backups, verify sender and domain, avoid/secure public Wi-Fi.

blocks.title: Practice
blocks.markdown:
Give the answer and a one-line reason.

1. Malware that self-replicates across a network with no host file and no user action.
2. A fraudulent phone call pretending to be the bank and asking you to read out a code.
3. An attacker on the same open Wi-Fi silently relaying and altering your traffic.
4. Flooding a website from thousands of machines so real users cannot reach it.
5. You get an SMS: "KYC pending, account will be frozen, click here." What is this, and what do you do?
6. Someone from "support" asks you to install a screen-sharing app to fix a problem. Safe or not?
7. A UPI notification says "accept to receive your ₹2,000 refund — enter UPI PIN." Should you?
8. Which is a server-side flaw a cautious user cannot avoid by being careful: shoulder surfing or SQL injection?

flashcards.front: Worm vs virus vs Trojan — how does each spread?
flashcards.back: Worm: self-replicates across a network, no host file or user action. Virus: attaches to a host file, spreads when that file is run and shared. Trojan: disguised as useful, runs only when the user opens it, and does not self-replicate.
flashcards.explanation: Self-replication is the divider examiners test.

flashcards.back: Phishing: a fraudulent message (usually email) impersonating a trusted body. Spear phishing: aimed at one named person using details about them. Vishing: by voice call. Smishing: by SMS.
flashcards.explanation: All are social engineering — tricking a person, not breaking a control.

flashcards.front: List the signs that an email is phishing.
flashcards.back: Sender domain not the real one, urgency or a threat, generic greeting, link text that doesn't match the real URL (hover to check), and a request for secrets like PIN, CVV or OTP.
flashcards.explanation: Reach the organisation through its official app or a printed number instead.

flashcards.front: What will a bank never ask a customer for?
flashcards.back: Full card number by email/call, PIN, CVV, online-banking password, or an OTP. Anyone asking — even if they know your name and last transaction — is an attacker.
flashcards.explanation: The OTP authorises the caller's transaction, not a 'verification'.

flashcards.front: Do you ever enter a UPI PIN to receive money?
flashcards.back: No. A UPI PIN only authorises money leaving your account. A 'collect request' or QR that asks for your PIN to 'accept a refund' is a scam to make you pay.
flashcards.explanation: Receiving money never needs your PIN.

flashcards.back: Both flood a service with traffic so genuine users cannot reach it. A DoS comes from one source; a DDoS comes from many machines at once, typically a botnet.
flashcards.explanation: It attacks availability, the A of the CIA triad.

flashcards.front: What is a man-in-the-middle attack, and what defeats the common form?
flashcards.back: An attacker secretly relays — and can alter — traffic between two parties who think they are talking directly, a risk on open Wi-Fi. HTTPS (TLS with a verified certificate) defeats the common form.
flashcards.explanation: A VPN also protects traffic on untrusted networks.

flashcards.front: Brute force vs dictionary attack vs credential stuffing?
flashcards.back: Brute force: try every possible password. Dictionary: try a list of likely passwords. Credential stuffing: reuse username/password pairs leaked from another breach.
flashcards.explanation: MFA and unique passwords blunt all three.
